questions.question: A compound C6H14 gives a 13C NMR spectrum with four peaks. Which compound gives this spectrum? The options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: 3-methylpentane, CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3, has four carbon environments.
steps: Four peaks means four different carbon environments; symmetry makes some carbons equivalent.
A (hexane): 3 environments, since C1 = C6, C2 = C5 and C3 = C4.
B (3-methylpentane): the two CH3 of the ethyl groups, the two CH2 groups, the CH and the CH3 branch give 4 environments.
C (2-methylpentane) has 5 environments and D (2,3-dimethylbutane) has only 2.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Cuminone, a flavouring, is shown as a structure. What is its molecular formula? Options A to D are given.
questions.answer: C: C11H14O
steps: Carbon count: 6 in the benzene ring, 1 in C=O, 1 in the CH3 of the acetyl group and 3 in the CH(CH3)2 group, so 11 C.
Hydrogen count: 4 on the ring (para-disubstituted), 3 in COCH3 and 7 in CH(CH3)2, so 14 H.
There is one O atom (the C=O).
The formula is C11H14O, option C.

questions.question: Which of the listed reactions is a redox reaction? The reactions are shown only in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: Cr2O7^2- + 2C -> Cr2O3 + CO3^2- + CO is the redox reaction.
steps: In A, Cr falls from +6 (Cr2O7^2-) to +3 (Cr2O3), so it is reduced.
In A, carbon rises from 0 to +4 (CO3^2-) and +2 (CO), so it is oxidised.
In B, C and D, Cr stays +6 and Cl stays -1 (or O stays -2): no oxidation numbers change.
B, C and D are substitution or acid-base type reactions, so only A is redox.

questions.question: Which species contains an element with the same oxidation number as bromine in KBrO3? A N2O5, B KMnO4, C K2FeO4, D Na2SO3.
questions.answer: A (N2O5): nitrogen is +5, the same as bromine in KBrO3.
steps: In KBrO3, K is +1 and each O is -2, so 1 + Br + 3(-2) = 0, giving Br = +5.
In N2O5, 2N + 5(-2) = 0, so each N = +5.
KMnO4 has Mn = +7; K2FeO4 has Fe = +6; Na2SO3 has S = +4.
Only N2O5 matches +5, so the answer is A.

questions.question: Complete the equation for Reaction 1 of the [Fe(H2O)6]3+ ion. The reagent for Reaction 1 is shown only in the diagram.
steps: NH3 acts as a base and removes H+ from three of the water ligands (deprotonation).
Each H+ removed gives an OH- ligand, so the neutral complex [Fe(H2O)3(OH)3] forms, the red-brown precipitate (iron(III) hydroxide).
The 3 H+ removed are accepted by 3 NH3 to give 3NH4+.
Check the charge: left side +3, right side 0 + 3(+1) = +3.

questions.question: State the type of reaction occurring in Reaction 2 on the [Fe(H2O)6]3+ solution.
questions.answer: Ligand substitution (ligand exchange).
steps: One H2O ligand is replaced by SCN-: [Fe(H2O)6]^3+ + SCN- -> [Fe(H2O)5SCN]^2+ + H2O.
The coordination number stays 6 and the oxidation state of Fe stays +3, so it is not redox or precipitation.

questions.question: Draw the structure of the complex ion formed in Reaction 3, showing all atoms. The reagent is shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: Octahedral [Fe(NH2CH2CH2NH2)3]^3+: three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands, each attached to Fe through both N atoms.
steps: Ethane-1,2-diamine is bidentate: both N atoms donate a lone pair to Fe^3+, so 3 ligands give 6 dative bonds.
Each ligand links two adjacent (cis) positions of the octahedron, forming a five-membered ring Fe-N-C-C-N.
Complete the diagram with three N-CH2-CH2-N chains joining the pairs of N atoms on the octahedron (two in the plane, two on wedges, two on dashes).
Show all atoms: each N has two H (NH2) and each C has two H (CH2), with N to Fe bonds shown as arrows or lines.
Mark the whole ion with a 3+ charge.

questions.question: Complete the table giving the colours of vanadium ions in oxidation states +2, +3, +4 and +5 in aqueous solution.
questions.answer: +3 green; +4 blue; +5 yellow (+2 is mauve, as given).
steps: V2+(aq) is mauve (violet), already given.
V3+(aq) is green.
V4+ (as VO^2+) is blue.
V5+ (as VO2+) is yellow.

questions.question: Two vanadium species are in equilibrium in aqueous solution. Deduce whether this is a redox reaction and justify using oxidation numbers.
questions.answer: Not a redox reaction: vanadium is +5 in both VO3^- and VO2^+.
steps: O stays -2 and H stays +1, so no oxidation number changes.
Therefore no electrons are transferred, and it is not a redox reaction.

questions.question: Predict an oxidising agent that converts V2+ to V3+ and then to V4+ but not to V5+, using only the data tables shown. Include equations and E values for the two reactions.
questions.answer: Nitrate ions in acid, NO3^-/NO2 (E = +0.80 V): V2+ + NO3^- + 2H+ -> V3+ + NO2 + H2O, Ecell = +1.06 V; V3+ + NO3^- -> VO^2+ + NO2, Ecell = +0.46 V.
steps: The oxidising agent must have E more positive than +0.34 V (V3+ to VO^2+) but less than +1.00 V (VO^2+ to VO2+).
Cu2+/Cu+ (+0.15 V) is too weak: it oxidises V2+ (-0.26 V) but not V3+ (+0.34 V). Br2/Br- (+1.09 V) is too strong: it would oxidise to V(V).
NO3^-/NO2 at +0.80 V lies between +0.34 V and +1.00 V, so it is the correct choice.
For VO^2+ to VO2+, Ecell = +0.80 - 1.00 = -0.20 V, so that step does not occur.

questions.question: Compare and contrast heterogeneous and homogeneous catalysis. Include one transition metal example of each type and a reaction in which it is used.
questions.answer: Heterogeneous: different phase, reactants adsorb on a solid surface (e.g. Fe in the Haber process). Homogeneous: same phase, catalyst forms intermediates via changing oxidation state (e.g. Fe2+ in iodide and peroxodisulfate reaction).
steps: Heterogeneous catalyst: in a different phase from the reactants, usually a solid with gas or liquid reactants.
Heterogeneous mechanism: reactants adsorb onto active sites on the surface, bonds weaken, and products desorb.
Example: iron in the Haber process, N2 + 3H2 to 2NH3, where a large surface area helps the rate.
Homogeneous catalyst: in the same phase as the reactants, so it mixes fully and forms intermediates.
Homogeneous mechanism: the transition metal changes oxidation state, e.g. S2O8^2- + 2Fe2+ gives 2SO4^2- + 2Fe3+, then 2Fe3+ + 2I- gives I2 + 2Fe2+.
Both types lower the activation energy and are regenerated, but heterogeneous rates depend on surface area and can be poisoned.

questions.topic: Amino Acid Structure at High pH
questions.question: Which structure best represents alanine at high pH? The options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: H3C-CH(NH2)-COO^-
steps: At high pH (alkaline) there is little H+, so the NH2 group is not protonated and stays as NH2.
The COOH group loses its proton to give COO-.
This is H2N-CH(CH3)-COO-, option B. A is the neutral molecule, C is the cation (low pH) and D is the zwitterion.

questions.question: Alanine is a crystalline solid at room temperature. What are the main forces broken when alanine melts? A London forces, B hydrogen bonds, C covalent bonds, D ionic bonds.
questions.answer: D (ionic bonds): the solid is a lattice of zwitterions held by electrostatic attraction.
steps: Amino acids exist as zwitterions in the solid state, with an NH3+ group and a COO- group.
Oppositely charged groups attract strongly, forming an ionic lattice.
Melting breaks these electrostatic attractions between ions.
Covalent bonds inside each molecule are not broken on melting.
London forces and hydrogen bonds are weaker, so they are not the main forces here.
Answer D.

questions.question: The repeat unit of a polymer is shown. Which statement is correct? A both a polypeptide and a polyamide, B neither, C polypeptide but not polyamide, D polyamide but not polypeptide.
questions.answer: D: a polyamide but not a polypeptide.
steps: The repeat unit is -CO-CH(CH3)-CO-NH-CH2CH2CH2-NH-, so it contains amide links -CONH-: it is a polyamide.
It is made from a dicarboxylic acid, HOOC-CH(CH3)-COOH, and a diamine, H2N(CH2)3NH2.
A polypeptide must be made from amino acids, with -NH-CH(R)-CO- units. Here the CH(CH3) carbon sits between two C=O groups, not next to N.
So it is a polyamide but not a polypeptide: D.

questions.question: Which structure best represents a hydrogen bond between methylamine and water? The options are diagrams in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: N lone pair bonded to the H of water, with a straight N...H-O line.
steps: The hydrogen bond forms between the lone pair on N of CH3NH2 and the delta+ H of an O-H bond in water.
The N, the H and the O should lie in a straight line (N...H-O angle about 180 degrees), which is shown in B.
A has the right atoms but a bent N...H-O arrangement.
C and D show a lone pair on O pointing at a H on carbon; C-H is not polar enough to hydrogen bond.

questions.question: Name the compound shown. Options: 1-methylpropanamide, 3-methylpropanamide, 2-methylbutanamide, 3-methylbutanamide.
questions.answer: C: 2-methylbutanamide
steps: The longest chain including the C(=O)NH2 carbon has 4 carbons, so the parent is butanamide.
The C=O carbon is C1 and the methyl branch is on the next carbon, C2.
So the name is 2-methylbutanamide, option C.

questions.question: The repeat unit of a polymer is shown. What is the structure of the monomer? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: propenamide, CH2=CH-CONH2.
steps: The polymer is an addition polymer with the repeat unit -CH2-CH(CONH2)-.
To find the monomer, replace the two chain bonds with a C=C double bond.
This gives CH2=CH-C(=O)NH2, propenamide (acrylamide), shown as A.
B, C and D have extra CH3 groups, so they do not match the repeat unit.

questions.question: Equal 0.1 mol dm-3 solutions of ammonia, butylamine and phenylamine are prepared. Which sequence shows them in order of increasing pH? A butylamine, phenylamine, ammonia; B ammonia, butylamine, phenylamine; C phenylamine, ammonia, butylamine; D ammonia, phenylamine, butylamine.
questions.answer: C (phenylamine, ammonia, butylamine): the weakest base gives the lowest pH.
steps: Alkyl groups donate electron density to N (positive inductive effect), so butylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
Butylamine is therefore the strongest base and gives the highest pH.
In phenylamine the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is the weakest base and gives the lowest pH.
Ammonia lies between the two, so increasing pH is phenylamine, ammonia, butylamine: option C.

questions.question: Which amine could not be prepared by reduction of a nitrile? The amine options are shown only in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: butan-2-amine (the NH2 is on a CH carbon with CH3 and C2H5 groups).
steps: Reducing a nitrile R-CN gives R-CH2-NH2, so the NH2 is always on a CH2 carbon (the former nitrile carbon).
A (butylamine), C ((CH3)2CHCH2NH2) and D ((CH3)3CCH2NH2) all have NH2 on a CH2 and can be made from the nitriles CH3CH2CH2CN, (CH3)2CHCN and (CH3)3CCN.
In B, the NH2 is on a carbon that carries a CH3 and a CH2CH3 group, so it cannot come from nitrile reduction.
The answer is B.

questions.question: How many different amino acids form the repeat unit of the polymer shown? Options are 3, 4, 5 and 6.
questions.answer: B: 4 different amino acids.
steps: Break the structure at each amide (peptide) link to identify the residues.
Reading along: alanine (side chain CH3), glycine (H), tyrosine (CH2C6H4OH), cysteine (CH2SH), glycine, alanine.
Alanine and glycine each appear twice, so there are four different amino acids: alanine, glycine, tyrosine and cysteine.

questions.question: Which type of compound cannot be a monomer in the formation of polyamides? A amides, B amino acids, C diacyl chlorides, D diamines.
questions.answer: A (amides): an amide has no pair of reactive groups to link in a chain.
steps: Polyamides form by condensation, so each monomer needs two reactive groups that form amide links.
Diamines and diacyl chlorides (or dicarboxylic acids) are the usual monomer pair.
Amino acids have both an amine and a carboxylic acid group, so they can link to form polyamides.
An amide already contains the C(=O)N group and does not have two reactive groups to join in a chain.
Answer A.

questions.question: Which sequence shows C6H5NH2, CH3CH2CH2NH2 and NH3 in order of decreasing basicity? Options A to D are given.
questions.answer: C: CH3CH2CH2NH2 > NH3 > C6H5NH2.
steps: Alkyl amines are stronger bases than NH3, because alkyl groups push electron density onto N.
So propylamine is more basic than ammonia.
Phenylamine is the weakest base because its N lone pair is delocalised into the ring.
Decreasing basicity: CH3CH2CH2NH2 > NH3 > C6H5NH2, which is option C.

questions.question: Deduce the classification (primary, secondary or tertiary) of the labelled amine group in chlorpheniramine.
questions.answer: Tertiary amine.
steps: The labelled N is bonded to three carbon atoms: two CH3 groups and the CH2 of the chain.
It has no N-H bond, so three alkyl groups on N means a tertiary amine.

questions.question: Pyridine is miscible with water and its solution is alkaline. Explain each of these properties.
questions.answer: Miscible: the N lone pair hydrogen-bonds with water. Alkaline: the lone pair accepts H+ from water, giving OH- ions (C5H5N + H2O to C5H5NH+ + OH-).
steps: Pyridine is a polar molecule with a lone pair on its nitrogen atom.
The N lone pair forms hydrogen bonds with O-H groups in water, so pyridine mixes with water in all proportions (miscible).
The N lone pair lies in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring, outside the delocalised pi system.
So the lone pair is available to accept a proton from water.
C5H5N + H2O to C5H5NH+ + OH- produces hydroxide ions.
The OH- ions make the solution alkaline (pH above 7).

questions.question: Complete the mechanism for the proposed reaction of monodesmethylchlorpheniramine with chloromethane, assuming it is similar to ammonia with chloromethane. Include curly arrows, dipoles and lone pairs.
questions.answer: Nucleophilic substitution: N lone pair attacks the delta+ C of CH3Cl, Cl- leaves, then H+ is lost from N to give R-N(CH3)-CH3 and HCl.
steps: Show the polar C-Cl bond with C delta+ and Cl delta-, and the lone pair on the N of R-NH-CH3.
Curly arrow 1: from the N lone pair to the delta+ carbon of CH3Cl.
Curly arrow 2: from the C-Cl bond to the Cl atom, so Cl- leaves. This gives the intermediate R(CH3)2NH+ (N now has four bonds and carries a + charge).
Curly arrow 3: from the N-H bond to N (the H leaves as H+, taken by Cl- or another amine molecule).
Products: tertiary amine R-N(CH3)2 (shown in the scheme) and HCl.

questions.question: Which ion forms when sodium nitrite and dilute HCl react with phenylamine at 5 C? The options are shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: the benzenediazonium ion, C6H5-N+ triple bond N.
steps: NaNO2 and dilute HCl make nitrous acid, HNO2, in situ.
At about 5 C, nitrous acid diazotises the primary aromatic amine C6H5NH2, giving C6H5N2+ Cl-.
The ion has the ring bonded to N+ with a triple bond to the second N (D). A and C are phenylammonium-type ions, and B puts the charge on the wrong N.

questions.question: Predict the structures of the two amino acid monomers that produce the part of a polymer shown in the diagram.
questions.answer: Methionine, H2N-CH(CH2CH2SCH3)-COOH, and glutamine, H2N-CH(CH2CH2CONH2)-COOH.
steps: Hydrolyse the amide (peptide) link: add H2O to the C-N bond so that the C=O side becomes COOH and the N side becomes NH2.
The left residue carries a CH2CH2-S-CH3 side chain: methionine.
The right residue carries a CH2CH2CONH2 side chain: glutamine.
Both monomers have the general form H2N-CH(R)-COOH.

questions.question: A repeat unit of an addition polymer used in food wraps is shown. Deduce the structures of the two monomers.
questions.answer: CH2=CCl2 (1,1-dichloroethene) and CH2=CHCl (chloroethene).
steps: The backbone is all C-C, so this is an addition polymer made from alkenes.
The four chain carbons split into two C2 units: -CCl2-CH2- and -CHCl-CH2-.
Restoring the C=C in each unit gives CH2=CCl2 and CH2=CHCl.

questions.question: A synthetic rubber has an approximate molar mass of 300 000 g mol-1. Calculate the approximate number of repeat units. The repeat unit structure is in the PDF.
questions.answer: About 1900 repeat units (1.9 x 10^3).
steps: The repeat unit is -CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH2-CH(C6H5)-, which has formula C12H14.
Molar mass of repeat unit = (12 x 12.0) + (14 x 1.0) = 158 g mol-1.
Number of repeat units = 300 000 / 158 = 1899, which is about 1900.

questions.question: The structure of crotonamide is shown. What is the repeat unit of the polymer formed from it? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: -CH(CH3)-CH(CONH2)- in the polymer backbone.
steps: Crotonamide, CH3CH=CHCONH2, contains a C=C, so it forms an addition polymer.
The C=C opens, leaving a two-carbon backbone with the CH3 and CONH2 groups as side groups.
The repeat unit is -CH(CH3)-CH(CONH2)-, option A.
B has a three-carbon backbone and C and D have the amide group in the chain, so they are wrong.

questions.question: Which ion is most likely to form when serine is dissolved in sodium carbonate solution? The options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: HOCH2-CH(NH2)-COO^-
steps: Sodium carbonate solution is mildly alkaline (a weak base).
It removes H+ from the acidic COOH group to give COO-.
The amine stays as NH2 (it is not protonated in alkali) and the alcohol OH is not acidic enough to lose H+ (so C is wrong).
This is HOCH2-CH(NH2)-COO-, option D.

questions.question: Serine melts at about 200 to 300 C. This high melting temperature is mainly due to the formation of: A hydrogen bonds, B ionic bonds, C London forces, D peptide bonds.
questions.answer: B (ionic bonds): serine exists as a zwitterion, and the ionic lattice needs a lot of energy to break.
steps: Serine, like other amino acids, exists as a zwitterion in the solid, with NH3+ and COO- groups.
Oppositely charged groups attract strongly, forming an ionic lattice.
Melting requires breaking these electrostatic attractions, which needs a high temperature.
London forces are weak and peptide bonds are within molecules, so they are not the main cause.
Answer B.

questions.question: Dilute HCl is added to butylamine and the solution is evaporated to dryness, giving a white solid. What is its formula? A CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl, B CH3CH2CH2CH2NH3Cl, C CH3CH2CH2CONH2, D CH3CH2CH2COOH.
questions.answer: B (CH3CH2CH2CH2NH3Cl): butylamine is neutralised to its ionic salt.
steps: Butylamine is a base, so its N lone pair accepts a proton from HCl.
CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2 + HCl gives CH3CH2CH2CH2NH3+ Cl-.
This ionic salt is a solid that remains when the solution is evaporated.
Option A is an alkyl chloride, C is an amide and D is a carboxylic acid, none of which form here.
Answer B.

questions.question: Amines can be prepared by reducing nitriles. Identify the nitrile and the reducing agent used to prepare butylamine.
questions.answer: C: butanenitrile, CH3CH2CH2CN, reduced by lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III), LiAlH4, in dry ether (H2 with a nickel catalyst would also work, but it is not offered).
steps: Reduction of a nitrile RCN gives a primary amine RCH2NH2, with the C of CN becoming CH2.
Butylamine is CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2, so the nitrile has R = CH3CH2CH2.
That nitrile is CH3CH2CH2CN, called butanenitrile.
Strong reducing agent: LiAlH4 in dry ether, followed by water work-up.
Alternative: hydrogen with a nickel catalyst.

questions.question: 2-aminopropanoic acid exists as a zwitterion at pH 6.0. What is its structure at pH 9.0? Options: A H2NCH(CH3)COOH, B H2NCH(CH3)COO-, C H3N+CH(CH3)COOH, D H3N+CH(CH3)COO-.
questions.answer: B (H2NCH(CH3)COO-): at pH 9 the NH3+ loses H+ and the COOH is ionised.
steps: At pH 6 the amino acid is a zwitterion, with NH3+ and COO-.
At pH 9 the solution is alkaline, with a high concentration of OH- ions.
The NH3+ group loses a proton to become NH2.
The COO- group is already ionised, so it stays as COO-.
The species is H2NCH(CH3)COO-, option B.

questions.question: What is the systematic name of isoleucine? A 2-amino-3-ethylbutanoic acid, B 2-amino-3-methylpentanoic acid, C 3-amino-2-ethylbutanoic acid, D 3-amino-2-methylpentanoic acid.
questions.answer: B: 2-amino-3-methylpentanoic acid.
steps: The longest chain includes the COOH carbon, so the parent is pentanoic acid (5 carbons).
The COOH carbon is C1 and the NH2 group is on C2.
The CH3 branch sits on C3, giving 3-methyl.
Name: 2-amino-3-methylpentanoic acid, option B.

questions.topic: Amino Acid Ion at Low pH
questions.question: What is the structure of isoleucine in a solution of pH 2?
questions.answer: CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH(NH3+)COOH, a cation with the amine protonated and the carboxylic acid un-ionised.
steps: At pH 2 there is a high concentration of H+ ions.
The amine group accepts a proton, forming NH3+.
The carboxylic acid is protonated, so it stays as COOH.
The overall charge is +1, giving CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH(NH3+)COOH.

questions.question: What are the reagents and conditions for Step 1 in the preparation of an azo dye from phenylamine? A NaNO2 and HCl at 5 C, B NaNO3 and HCl at 5 C, C NaNO2 and HCl at 50 C, D NaNO3 and HCl at 50 C.
questions.answer: A: NaNO2 and HCl at 5 C.
steps: Diazotisation uses nitrite ions, from sodium nitrite, reacting with HCl to form nitrous acid, HNO2.
Nitrate (NaNO3) cannot form nitrous acid, so options B and D are wrong.
The diazonium ion is unstable above about 5 C, so 50 C is wrong.
Answer A.

questions.question: Which reagent and condition are used for Step 2 in the azo dye scheme?
questions.answer: B: naphthalen-2-ol (2-naphthol) dissolved in alkaline solution, kept cold (below 10 C).
steps: Step 2 is azo coupling: the diazonium ion is a weak electrophile and attacks an activated aromatic ring.
In the dye, the OH is on C2 and the N=N is on C1 of naphthalene, so the coupling partner is naphthalen-2-ol (A or B), not naphthalen-1-ol (C or D).
Alkaline conditions turn the phenol-type OH into O-, which makes the ring much more reactive, so alkaline (B) is needed, not acidic.
The mixture is kept at about 5 C so the diazonium ion does not decompose.

questions.question: Step 1 uses concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids at 55 C. Why is the reaction not carried out at 80 C? A further substitution by a nitro group occurs, B nitrobenzene decomposes, C substitution by SO3H occurs, D the nitric acid decomposes.
questions.answer: A: higher temperature allows a further nitro group to substitute (dinitration).
steps: Nitration of benzene is an electrophilic substitution with NO2+.
A nitro group is deactivating, but at higher temperatures a second nitration still occurs.
So a second nitro group is added to the ring at 80 C, giving dinitro compounds.
Temperature control at 55 C keeps the product as mononitrobenzene: answer A.

questions.question: How is Step 2 carried out (reduction of nitrobenzene to phenylamine)? A Sn, concentrated HCl(aq) and NaOH(aq) added together, B Sn, dilute HCl(aq) and NaOH(aq) added together, C Sn and concentrated HCl(aq) added first, then NaOH(aq) at the end, D Sn and dilute HCl(aq) added first, then NaOH(aq) at the end.
questions.answer: C: Sn and concentrated HCl first, then NaOH added at the end.
steps: Tin with concentrated HCl reduces the nitro group, NO2, to NH3+ in acid.
Concentrated acid is needed for the reduction to go to completion.
NaOH is added only at the end to neutralise the acid and release free phenylamine.
Adding NaOH first would stop the reduction, so options A and B are wrong.
Answer C.

questions.question: Step 3 uses sodium nitrite and dilute HCl at 5 C. Which is the structure of intermediate L? Options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: benzenediazonium chloride, C6H5-N+ triple bond N, Cl-.
steps: Step 3 is diazotisation: NaNO2 with dilute HCl at 5 C converts the primary aromatic amine to a diazonium salt.
The ion is C6H5-N2+ with Cl- as a separate counter-ion: the two N atoms are joined by a triple bond and the ring-bonded N carries the + charge.
A and C show a covalent N-Cl bond, which is wrong, and D shows N+=N with a double bond, which is wrong.
The answer is B.

questions.question: The reactant in Step 4 is phenol. What condition is needed for this reaction? A acidic, B alkaline, C ethanolic, D neutral.
questions.answer: B (alkaline): phenol is converted to phenoxide ion, which couples with the diazonium ion.
steps: Azo coupling needs an activated, electron-rich ring to attack the diazonium ion.
In alkaline solution phenol is deprotonated to the phenoxide ion, which is much more reactive.
Acidic or neutral conditions leave phenol unionised and coupling is slow.
Answer B.

questions.question: Name the three functional groups present in benzocaine.
questions.answer: Ester, primary amine (aromatic) and benzene ring (arene).
steps: The -COO-CH2CH3 group is an ester.
The -NH2 attached to the ring is a primary (aromatic) amine.
The six-membered ring with delocalised electrons is a benzene ring (arene).

questions.question: Write an equation, using molecular formulae, for procaine reacting with hydrochloric acid to form a monohydrochloride salt.
questions.answer: C13H20N2O2 + HCl -> C13H21N2O2Cl
steps: Procaine formula: C 13 (6 ring + 1 C=O + 2 in OCH2CH2 + 4 in the two ethyl groups); H 20 (4 ring + 2 in NH2 + 4 in OCH2CH2 + 10 in the ethyl groups); N2; O2.
Procaine is C13H20N2O2. A monohydrochloride salt adds one HCl.
Equation: C13H20N2O2 + HCl -> C13H21N2O2Cl (or C13H20N2O2.HCl).

questions.question: Explain, by considering both nitrogen atoms in procaine, which is more likely to be protonated by HCl.
questions.answer: The tertiary (diethylamino) nitrogen is protonated, because its lone pair is more available than that of the aromatic NH2.
steps: The tertiary amine N is attached to alkyl groups, which push electron density onto N (positive inductive effect). Its lone pair is available to accept H+.
The aromatic NH2 lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring (and the ring is joined to the electron-withdrawing ester), so it is less available.
So the diethylamino nitrogen is the stronger base and is the one protonated by HCl.

questions.question: When benzocaine and procaine are hydrolysed, one product is the same in both reactions. Give its structure.
questions.answer: 4-aminobenzoic acid, H2N-C6H4-COOH.
steps: Hydrolysis of the ester group splits the molecule into an acid and an alcohol.
Benzocaine gives 4-aminobenzoic acid and ethanol; procaine gives 4-aminobenzoic acid and 2-(diethylamino)ethanol.
The product common to both is 4-aminobenzoic acid (HOOC attached to the ring, with NH2 para to it).

questions.question: Give the mechanism for Step 1 of the lidocaine synthesis, including an equation for formation of the electrophile.
questions.answer: Electrophilic substitution: NO2+ is made from HNO3 and H2SO4, attacks the ring to form an arenium ion, then loses H+ to give 2,6-dimethylnitrobenzene.
steps: Formation of the electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4- (or HNO3 + H2SO4 -> NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O).
Curly arrow from the delocalised ring electrons (a C=C of 1,3-dimethylbenzene) to the N atom of NO2+, at the carbon between the two CH3 groups.
This forms an arenium ion intermediate: the ring is broken (horseshoe) with a + charge, and the carbon bonded to NO2 still has an H.
Curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring, releasing H+ and restoring aromaticity, giving 2,6-dimethylnitrobenzene.
The H+ reacts with HSO4- to regenerate H2SO4 (the catalyst).

questions.question: A low yield of 2,6-dimethylnitrobenzene forms in Step 1 due to additional organic products. Give possible structures for two of them.
questions.answer: Any two of: 2,4-dimethylnitrobenzene (1,3-dimethyl-4-nitrobenzene), 3,5-dimethylnitrobenzene (1,3-dimethyl-5-nitrobenzene), or a dinitro compound such as 1,3-dimethyl-4,6-dinitrobenzene.
steps: The nitronium ion can attack other positions of 1,3-dimethylbenzene, giving isomeric mononitro products.
Attack at C4 (para to one CH3 and ortho to the other) gives 2,4-dimethylnitrobenzene.
Attack at C5 (meta to both CH3) gives 3,5-dimethylnitrobenzene.
A second nitration of the product gives dinitro compounds such as 1,3-dimethyl-4,6-dinitrobenzene.

questions.question: Give the reagents for Step 2 in the lidocaine synthesis.
questions.answer: Tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid (heat under reflux), then NaOH(aq).
steps: Step 2 reduces the nitro group NO2 on the ring to NH2.
Reagents: Sn with concentrated HCl, heated under reflux. This gives the ammonium salt.
Add NaOH(aq) at the end to release the free amine, 2,6-dimethylphenylamine.
H2 with a nickel catalyst is an alternative.

questions.question: Deduce the skeletal formula of the reagent for Step 3 in the lidocaine synthesis.
questions.answer: Chloroethanoyl chloride, ClCH2COCl: Cl-CH2-C(=O)-Cl drawn as a skeletal formula (a CH2 carbon bonded to Cl, then a C=O carbon bearing a second Cl).
steps: Step 3 converts the arylamine ArNH2 into the amide ArNHC(=O)CH2Cl.
The new group is an acyl group -C(=O)CH2Cl, so the reagent is an acyl chloride.
The reagent is ClCH2COCl: skeletal formula Cl-CH2 joined to C(=O)Cl.
The acyl chloride C-Cl bond is much more reactive than the CH2-Cl bond, so the NH2 attacks the C=O carbon.

questions.question: State the type and mechanism of the reaction in Step 4 of the lidocaine synthesis.
questions.answer: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2).
steps: Diethylamine, (C2H5)2NH, has a lone pair on N, so it acts as a nucleophile.
It attacks the delta+ carbon of the CH2-Cl group and replaces the chlorine.
The mechanism is a one-step bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2), giving lidocaine and HCl.

questions.question: Indicate any chiral centres on the structure of articaine.
questions.answer: The one chiral centre is the CH carbon in the side chain, bonded to CH3, H, NH-CH2CH2CH3 and C(=O)NH-ring.
steps: A chiral centre is a carbon atom with four different groups attached.
The carbon carrying the CH3 (drawn with the methyl pointing down) is bonded to H, CH3, NH-propyl and C(=O)NH-ring, which are all different.
Ring carbons are sp2, and the other carbons have two identical groups (such as CH2 and CH3), so there is only this one chiral centre.

questions.question: Articaine has a half-life of 20 minutes. A 100 mg dose is given. Calculate the mass in micrograms remaining after 4 hours. Use 1 mg = 10^-3 g.
questions.answer: 24.4 micrograms (about 2.44 x 10^-2 mg remains after 12 half-lives).
steps: Time = 4 h = 240 min.
Number of half-lives = 240 / 20 = 12.
Convert to micrograms: 0.02441 mg = 24.4 micrograms (1 microgram = 10^-6 g).

questions.question: A protein was hydrolysed and analysed by thin-layer chromatography. What is the best estimate of the Rf value of amino acid X? Options 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8.
steps: Rf = distance moved by the spot / distance moved by the solvent front, both measured from the baseline.
Measuring the diagram, spot X is about 56% of the way from the baseline to the solvent front (roughly 12 of 21 equal divisions).
Rf = 0.56, which is closest to 0.6 (option C).

questions.question: Which reaction can form a secondary amine? The options are reaction schemes in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: C2H5NH2 + C2H5Br gives the secondary amine (C2H5)2NH.
steps: Bromoethane substitutes one H on the N of the primary amine C2H5NH2, giving (C2H5)2NH, a secondary amine (nucleophilic substitution).
A: reducing benzonitrile with LiAlH4 gives the primary amine C6H5CH2NH2.
C: (C2H5)2NH + C2H5Br gives the tertiary amine (C2H5)3N.
D: NaOH hydrolyses the amide to a carboxylate and a primary amine, ethylamine.
So only B forms a secondary amine.

questions.question: Four amino acids are dissolved to give separate 0.05 mol dm-3 solutions. Which gives the lowest pH? The amino acid options are shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: glutamic acid (2-aminopentanedioic acid).
steps: The lowest pH comes from the amino acid with the extra acidic group.
B has a second COOH group in the side chain, which can donate H+ to water, making the solution most acidic.
A (serine) and D (tryptophan) have neutral side chains and give solutions near neutral, and C (lysine) has an extra NH2, which makes the solution basic.

questions.question: Complete the electronic configurations for a manganese atom and a manganese(II) ion, using electron-in-box notation.
questions.answer: Mn: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5 4s2; Mn2+: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5 (5 unpaired electrons in 3d).
steps: Mn has 25 electrons, so the configuration is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5 4s2.
In boxes: the five 3d orbitals each hold one electron (parallel spins), and 4s holds a pair.
Mn2+ loses both 4s electrons first, leaving 3d5 with five unpaired electrons.
The half-filled 3d5 sub-shell is especially stable.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of electron configurations, why the E value for the Mn2+/Mn3+ half-cell is much higher than that for the Fe2+/Fe3+ half-cell.
questions.answer: Mn2+ (3d5) is a stable half-filled sub-shell, so Mn3+ (3d4) is readily reduced to it. Fe3+ (3d5) is already stable and resists reduction, so the Fe3+/Fe2+ potential is lower.
steps: The half-cell is Mn3+ + e- to Mn2+ (reduction), and a higher E means Mn3+ is more easily reduced.
Mn2+ is 3d5, a half-filled sub-shell with extra stability.
Mn3+ is 3d4, so gaining one electron to reach 3d5 is favourable.
Fe3+ is 3d5 (already stable), so it is less willing to gain an electron.
Hence the Fe3+/Fe2+ potential is lower than the Mn3+/Mn2+ potential.

questions.question: Chlorine is made by MnO2 + 4HCl to MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O. Explain, in terms of oxidation numbers, why this is a redox reaction.
questions.answer: Mn falls from +4 to +2 (reduced); Cl rises from -1 to 0 (oxidised).
steps: In MnO2, Mn = +4 (O is -2 each).
In MnCl2, Mn = +2, so Mn gains electrons and is reduced.
In HCl, Cl = -1; in Cl2 the oxidation number is 0, so Cl loses electrons and is oxidised.
A change in oxidation numbers of both species shows a redox reaction.

questions.question: 100 cm3 of hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes to give 86.0 cm3 of oxygen at r.t.p. (molar volume 24.0 dm3 mol-1). Calculate the concentration in mol dm-3. Equation: 2H2O2 to 2H2O + O2.
steps: Moles of O2 = 0.0860 dm3 / 24.0 dm3 mol-1 = 3.58 x 10^-3 mol.
From 2H2O2 to O2, moles of H2O2 = 2 x 3.58 x 10^-3 = 7.17 x 10^-3 mol.
Volume of solution = 0.100 dm3.
Concentration = 7.17 x 10^-3 / 0.100 = 0.0717 mol dm-3.

questions.question: In acid, manganate(VI) ions disproportionate to manganate(VII) ions and manganese(IV) oxide. Write the ionic equation (state symbols not required).
questions.answer: 3MnO4^2- + 4H+ to 2MnO4- + MnO2 + 2H2O
steps: Mn in MnO4^2- is +6; it is oxidised to +7 in MnO4- and reduced to +4 in MnO2.
Oxidation: 2MnO4^2- to 2MnO4- + 2e-.
Reduction: MnO4^2- + 4H+ + 2e- to MnO2 + 2H2O.
Adding them gives 3MnO4^2- + 4H+ to 2MnO4- + MnO2 + 2H2O; charges (-2 each side) and atoms balance.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of catalysis, why the two concentration-time graphs for the manganate(VII) and ethanedioate reaction have different shapes (Experiment 2 adds manganese(II) sulfate).
questions.answer: Mn2+ is formed in the reaction and acts as a catalyst (autocatalysis), so Experiment 1 starts slowly and speeds up, but Experiment 2 contains Mn2+ at the start and is fast immediately.
steps: Experiment 1: the graph is flat at first, then steepens. At the start there is no Mn2+, and the reaction between two negative ions (MnO4- and C2O4^2-) is slow because they repel.

Mn2+ is a product of the reaction. As it builds up it acts as a homogeneous catalyst (autocatalysis), providing a lower activation energy route, so the rate increases and the curve gets steeper before levelling off as reactants are used up.
Experiment 2: Mn2+ is added at the start, so the catalysed route works from the beginning. The gradient is steepest at time zero.
The rate then falls steadily as the MnO4- concentration decreases, giving a curve that starts steep and flattens.
Catalysis route: Mn2+ reacts with MnO4- to form Mn3+, and Mn3+ then oxidises C2O4^2- and returns to Mn2+.

questions.question: 1.73 g of methylbenzene (Mr 92) is heated with 7.00 g of KMnO4 (Mr 158) and excess KOH. Show that KMnO4 is in excess.
questions.answer: 0.0443 mol KMnO4 is available but only 0.0376 mol is needed, so KMnO4 is in excess.
steps: Moles of methylbenzene = 1.73 / 92 = 0.0188 mol.
Moles of KMnO4 = 7.00 / 158 = 0.0443 mol.
Oxidising CH3 to COO- takes 6 electrons per molecule, while each MnO4- to MnO2 takes 3, so 2 mol KMnO4 per mol methylbenzene.
KMnO4 needed = 2 x 0.0188 = 0.0376 mol.
0.0443 mol is more than 0.0376 mol, so KMnO4 is in excess.

questions.question: State how benzoate ions, C6H5COO-, can be converted into benzoic acid.
questions.answer: Acidify the solution with dilute acid such as HCl(aq) or H2SO4(aq): C6H5COO- + H+ to C6H5COOH.
steps: Benzoate is the conjugate base of benzoic acid.
Adding a dilute strong acid supplies H+ ions.
The benzoate ion is protonated to form C6H5COOH.
Benzoic acid is only slightly soluble in cold water, so it separates out as a solid.

questions.question: Write the half-equations for the anode (zinc alloy) and the cathode (manganese(IV) oxide) of an alkaline cell with KOH electrolyte.
questions.answer: Anode: Zn + 2OH- to ZnO + H2O + 2e-. Cathode: 2MnO2 + H2O + 2e- to Mn2O3 + 2OH-.
steps: Anode: zinc is oxidised from 0 to +2 in ZnO, losing 2 electrons.
OH- supplies the oxygen and balances the hydrogen: Zn + 2OH- to ZnO + H2O + 2e-.
Cathode: Mn falls from +4 to +3 in Mn2O3, gaining one electron per Mn, so 2 electrons overall for 2 MnO2.
2MnO2 + H2O + 2e- to Mn2O3 + 2OH- balances O, H and charge.
Adding the half-equations gives Zn + 2MnO2 to ZnO + Mn2O3.

questions.question: The standard electrode potential for the Zn/ZnO half-cell is -1.28 V. Calculate the standard electrode potential for the MnO2/Mn2O3 half-cell.
steps: Ecell = E(cathode) - E(anode), and the cell reaction has Ecell = +1.43 V.
MnO2 is reduced at the cathode and Zn is oxidised at the anode, so the anode potential is -1.28 V.

questions.question: Draw a mechanism for the reaction of phenol with dilute nitric acid to form 2-nitrophenol, assuming NO2+ is the electrophile.
questions.answer: NO2+ attacks the ring at the position ortho to OH, forming an arenium ion; H+ is lost to restore the aromatic ring.
steps: NO2+ is the electrophile; the pi electrons of the ring attack its N atom (curly arrow from C=C to N).
The ring carbon ortho to the OH group bonds to NO2, giving a positive arenium (Wheland) intermediate.
The positive charge is delocalised over the ring and stabilised by the lone pair on the OH oxygen.
A base (e.g. H2O or NO3-) removes H+ from the carbon bearing NO2.
The C-H electrons return to the ring, restoring aromaticity and giving 2-nitrophenol.

questions.question: Explain why phenol requires milder conditions for nitration than benzene, which needs concentrated HNO3 and H2SO4 at 60 C.
questions.answer: The O lone pair on the OH group donates electron density into the ring, activating it towards electrophilic attack, so milder conditions are enough.
steps: The lone pair on the O atom of the OH group is delocalised into the benzene ring.
This increases electron density in the ring, making it more nucleophilic.
The ring is therefore more readily attacked by the weak electrophile NO2+.
So dilute nitric acid at room temperature is sufficient, unlike benzene.

questions.question: Devise a synthesis of N-phenylethylethanamide from (bromomethyl)benzene without a Grignard reagent, including reagents, conditions and intermediates. Interpreted as CH3CONHCH2CH2C6H5.
questions.answer: C6H5CH2Br to C6H5CH2CN (KCN, ethanol, reflux) to C6H5CH2CH2NH2 (LiAlH4, dry ether) to CH3CONHCH2CH2C6H5 (CH3COCl).
steps: Step 1: PhCH2Br + KCN in ethanol under reflux, nucleophilic substitution, giving phenylethanenitrile PhCH2CN (carbon chain lengthened by one).
Step 2: reduce the nitrile with LiAlH4 in dry ether (or H2 with Ni), giving 2-phenylethylamine, PhCH2CH2NH2.
Step 3: react the primary amine with ethanoyl chloride, CH3COCl, at room temperature.
This is nucleophilic addition-elimination, forming the amide CH3CONHCH2CH2C6H5 and HCl.
Use a base or excess amine to neutralise the HCl formed.

questions.question: Complete the structure of the zwitterion of phenylalanine.
questions.answer: C6H5CH2CH(NH3+)COO-, with the COOH proton transferred to the NH2 group.
steps: Phenylalanine has an NH2 group and a COOH group on the same carbon.
In the zwitterion, the acidic COOH loses its proton to the basic NH2.
This gives NH3+ and COO-, with no overall charge.
Zwitterion: C6H5CH2CH(NH3+)COO-.

questions.question: Draw the structure of the dipeptide formed from phenylalanine.
questions.answer: C6H5CH2CH(NH2)CONHCH(CH2C6H5)COOH (phenylalanylphenylalanine).
steps: A peptide bond forms between the COOH group of one phenylalanine and the NH2 group of another.
Water is eliminated (condensation).
The C=O carbon of one residue bonds to the N of the other, giving -CO-NH-.
The result is C6H5CH2CH(NH2)CONHCH(CH2C6H5)COOH.

questions.question: Give the molecular formula of aspartame.
questions.answer: C14H18N2O5 (molar mass 294 g mol-1).
steps: Aspartame is the dipeptide-type molecule formed from aspartic acid and phenylalanine, with a methyl ester group.
Check against the molar mass of 294 g mol-1 given later in the question.
Total = 294, so the formula C14H18N2O5 is consistent.

questions.question: Circle the two chiral carbon atoms in aspartame on the structure shown.
questions.answer: The two chiral carbons are the alpha carbons (the CH carbons bonded to N) of the phenylalanine unit and of the aspartic acid unit.
steps: A chiral carbon has four different groups attached.
Phenylalanine unit: the CH bonded to CH2C6H5, NH (peptide N), COOCH3 and H.
Aspartic acid unit: the CH bonded to NH2, CH2COOH, C(=O)NH and H.
Circle these two CH carbons. All the other carbons have repeated groups (CH2, CH3) or are sp2.

questions.question: Aspartame is hydrolysed by hydrochloric acid in the stomach. Draw the structures of the three organic products of complete acid hydrolysis.
questions.answer: Aspartic acid HOOCCH2CH(NH2)COOH, phenylalanine C6H5CH2CH(NH2)COOH and methanol CH3OH.
steps: Acid hydrolysis breaks the peptide (amide) link, adding H2O across C-N.
It also hydrolyses the methyl ester (COOCH3), giving a COOH group and methanol.
Products: aspartic acid, phenylalanine and methanol (in HCl the amino acids exist as NH3+ Cl- salts, which is also acceptable).

questions.question: A fizzy drink contains 53 mg of aspartame per 100 cm3. Calculate the number of aspartame molecules in a 330 cm3 can. Molar mass 294 g mol-1; Avogadro constant 6.02 x 10^23 mol-1.
questions.answer: 3.6 x 10^20 molecules
steps: Limited by 2 significant figures (53 and 330), so the answer is 3.6 x 10^20 molecules.

questions.question: A polyamide has the repeat unit shown. Which monomers can form it? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl dichloride (ClOC-C6H4-COCl) and benzene-1,4-diamine (H2N-C6H4-NH2).
steps: The repeat unit -CO-C6H4-CO-NH-C6H4-NH- contains amide links, so it is a polyamide formed by condensation polymerisation.
The C=O side comes from a diacyl chloride (or dicarboxylic acid), the N side from a diamine.
These are ClOC-C6H4-COCl and H2N-C6H4-NH2, both 1,4-substituted: option D.
A is a single amino acid and would give a different repeat unit. B is a diamide and C is a diamide with a diol, which do not form this polymer.

questions.question: Compound X reacts with excess nitrous acid, then couples with excess phenol to form an azo dye. What is the structure of the dye? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: both NH2 groups become azo links to a 4-hydroxyphenyl group.
steps: Excess nitrous acid converts both primary aromatic NH2 groups of X into diazonium groups (N2+).
Excess phenol then couples with each diazonium group, giving azo links (-N=N-) at the position para to the OH of phenol.
So the dye has an HO-C6H4-N=N- group at each end of the dimethoxybiphenyl unit, structure D.
A and B have no N=N links and C has only one azo group.

questions.question: Which of these is the weakest base? A ammonia, B butylamine, C ethylamine, D phenylamine.
questions.answer: D (phenylamine).
steps: Alkylamines (butylamine, ethylamine) are stronger bases than ammonia, because alkyl groups donate electron density to N.
In phenylamine the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, making it much less available to accept H+.
So phenylamine is the weakest base.

questions.question: Write the equation for the reaction of glycine with sodium hydroxide (state symbols not required).
questions.answer: H2NCH2COOH + NaOH to H2NCH2COONa + H2O
steps: The COOH group of glycine is acidic and is neutralised by NaOH.
Products: the sodium salt of the carboxylate and water.
The amine group is not affected by NaOH.

questions.question: Calculate the volume, in cm3, of 0.100 mol dm-3 HCl that completely reacts with 1.825 g of lysine (Mr = 146).
steps: Moles of lysine = 1.825 / 146 = 0.0125 mol.
Lysine has two amine groups, each reacting with one H+, so 2 mol HCl per mol lysine.
Moles of HCl = 2 x 0.0125 = 0.0250 mol.

questions.question: Draw three-dimensional diagrams of the two optically active enantiomers of lysine.
questions.answer: Two mirror-image tetrahedral drawings of H2N-CH((CH2)4NH2)-COOH about the alpha carbon.
steps: The alpha carbon is bonded to four different groups: NH2, COOH, H and (CH2)4NH2.
Draw one enantiomer with two bonds in the plane, one wedge and one dash, e.g. COOH and (CH2)4NH2 in the plane, NH2 on a wedge and H on a dash.
Draw the other as its mirror image: swap the NH2 and H (wedge and dash), or reflect through a mirror line between the two drawings.
The two drawings cannot be superimposed.

questions.question: Describe how the two optically active enantiomers of lysine could be distinguished (practical details not required).
questions.answer: Use polarimetry: each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light by the same amount but in opposite directions.
steps: Pass plane-polarised light through a sample of each enantiomer in a polarimeter.
One enantiomer rotates the plane clockwise (+) and the other anticlockwise (-).
The rotation angles are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the two are distinguished by their sign of rotation.

questions.question: State why glycine does not exist as enantiomers.
questions.answer: Glycine has no chiral centre: its alpha carbon carries two H atoms, so the molecule is not asymmetric.
steps: A chiral centre needs four different groups attached to one carbon.
The alpha carbon of glycine is CH2, with two identical H atoms.
Its mirror image is superimposable on it, so there are no enantiomers.

questions.question: Draw spots on the chromatogram to show glycine (Rf 0.26) and lysine (Rf 0.14).
questions.answer: Two spots in a vertical line above the mixture spot: glycine at 0.26 of the distance from origin to solvent front, lysine at 0.14.
steps: The grid has 10 equal divisions from the origin to the solvent front, so each division is 0.1 in Rf.
Glycine, Rf 0.26: draw a spot 2.6 divisions above the origin (just over halfway between the 2nd and 3rd lines).
Lysine, Rf 0.14: draw a spot 1.4 divisions above the origin (between the 1st and 2nd lines).
Both spots are on the vertical line through the mixture spot, and the glycine spot is higher than lysine.

questions.question: Draw a different dipeptide of glycine and lysine from the one shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: Example: Gly-Lys, H2NCH2CONH-CH[(CH2)4NH2]COOH (or Lys-Gly if Gly-Lys is the one drawn).
steps: A dipeptide has one peptide bond formed between COOH of one amino acid and NH2 of the other.
Glycine-lysine: the COOH of glycine links to the alpha NH2 of lysine.
The alpha COOH of lysine is left free, and the side-chain NH2 is unchanged.
A different dipeptide is the reverse order, lysine-glycine, if the drawn one is glycine-lysine.

questions.question: Identify the correct trend of increasing strength as a base. A C6H5NH2 < NH3 < CH3NH2, B C6H5NH2 < CH3NH2 < NH3, C NH3 < CH3NH2 < C6H5NH2, D NH3 < C6H5NH2 < CH3NH2.
questions.answer: A: C6H5NH2 < NH3 < CH3NH2.
steps: Methylamine is more basic than ammonia, because the CH3 group donates electrons to N.
Phenylamine is the weakest, because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring.
So increasing strength is C6H5NH2 < NH3 < CH3NH2, option A.

questions.question: State the starting materials that can be used to make benzenediazonium ions. The options are shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: HNO2 and phenylamine (C6H5NH2).
steps: A diazonium ion forms when nitrous acid, HNO2, reacts with a primary aromatic amine at about 5 C.
Phenylamine C6H5NH2 supplies the ring and the N, giving C6H5N2+.
Nitrobenzene is not an amine, and HNO3 is nitric acid, not nitrous acid, so B, C and D are wrong.

questions.question: Draw the structure of the azo dye formed when benzenediazonium ions react with phenol.
questions.answer: B: 4-(phenyldiazenyl)phenol, HO-C6H4-N=N-C6H5.
steps: Coupling happens at the position para to the OH of phenol, where the ring is most activated.
The benzenediazonium ion joins the phenol ring through an azo link, -N=N-, with no loss of the OH.
This is HO-C6H4-N=N-C6H5, option B. A has NH-NH, C has an NH link and D has a biphenyl link.

questions.question: Which combination of reactants will produce a primary aliphatic amine as the product? The options are shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: (CH3)2CHCN with Ni/H2 gives (CH3)2CHCH2NH2.
steps: Hydrogen with a nickel catalyst reduces a nitrile R-CN to R-CH2-NH2, a primary amine.
Here R is an aliphatic group, CH(CH3)2, so the product is a primary aliphatic amine.
B (2-bromobutane + CH3NH2) forms a secondary amine, C gives phenylamine (aromatic), and D gives N-ethylphenylamine (a secondary aromatic amine).

questions.topic: Making an Amide in One Step
questions.question: Which equation shows the two compounds that react to produce ethanamide, CH3CONH2, in a single step? A CH4 + HCONH2, B CH3COOH + NH3, C CH3COCl + NH3, D CH3CHO + NH3.
questions.answer: C: CH3COCl + NH3 to CH3CONH2 + HCl.
steps: Ethanoyl chloride is an acyl chloride, the most reactive acyl compound for making amides.
Ammonia attacks the C of C=O, and chloride is eliminated (addition-elimination), giving CH3CONH2 and HCl.
Option B needs heating and forms a salt first, and option A and D are not balanced correctly.
Answer C.

questions.question: Which form of aspartic acid is formed at pH 12? The options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: C: the ion with NH2 and both carboxylate groups (COO-).
steps: At pH 12 the solution is strongly alkaline, so both COOH groups lose H+ to give COO-.
The NH3+ group also loses H+ to become NH2.
So the form is H2N-CH(CH2COO-)-COO-, option C.

questions.question: Which is a correct structure when aspartic acid forms a dipeptide with glutamine? Options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: the dipeptide with the peptide bond between the alpha COOH of aspartic acid and the NH2 of glutamine.
steps: A peptide bond forms when the alpha COOH of aspartic acid joins the alpha NH2 of glutamine, with loss of water.
In D, HOOC-CH2-CH(NH2)-CO-NH-CH(COOH)-CH2CH2-CONH2, the aspartic acid side-chain COOH and the glutamine side-chain amide are unchanged.
B uses the side-chain COOH of aspartic acid to form the bond, which is not the normal peptide link.
A and C have the N bonded between two C=O groups and lose the glutamine amide NH2, so they are wrong.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of chiral centres in the dipeptides in (b)(i) formed from aspartic acid and glutamine? A 0, B 1, C 2, D 3.
questions.answer: C (2): one chiral alpha carbon in each residue.
steps: A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups.
Each amino acid except glycine has a chiral alpha carbon: aspartic acid and glutamine each contribute one.
The side chains (CH2COOH and CH2CH2CONH2) have no chiral carbons.
The peptide link does not create a new chiral centre, so the maximum is 2.

questions.topic: Hydrogen Bonding of Butylamine to Water
questions.question: Butylamine is miscible with water. Draw a labelled diagram of one intermolecular interaction between butylamine and water, including lone pairs and dipoles.
questions.answer: A hydrogen bond between the N lone pair of butylamine (delta-) and an O-H hydrogen of water (delta+), drawn as a dotted line, with lone pairs and dipoles labelled.
steps: N in butylamine has a lone pair and is partially negative (delta-).
The O-H hydrogen of water is partially positive (delta+).
Draw the N lone pair pointing towards the H of O-H (or the O lone pair of water to an N-H hydrogen of butylamine).
Label the dipoles and lone pairs and show the hydrogen bond as a dotted line.

questions.question: The exposure limit for butylamine is 15 mg m-3. Calculate the maximum number of butylamine molecules allowed per cubic metre (L = 6.02 x 10^23 mol-1).
questions.answer: 1.2 x 10^20 molecules per m3
steps: Mass limit = 15 mg m-3 = 0.015 g m-3.
Molecules = 2.05 x 10^-4 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.24 x 10^20, i.e. 1.2 x 10^20 to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: Butylamine reacts with ethanoyl chloride to form N-butylethanamide. Write the equation using displayed formulae.
questions.answer: CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2 + CH3COCl to CH3CONHCH2CH2CH2CH3 + HCl (show displayed formulae in the answer).
steps: The lone pair on the N of butylamine attacks the C of the C=O in ethanoyl chloride.
The Cl- leaves, and a proton is lost from N, giving the amide.
Products: N-butylethanamide and hydrogen chloride.
Write the displayed formulae for each species, with the N-H and C=O shown.

questions.question: Explain why butylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
questions.answer: The butyl group is electron-donating (positive inductive effect), raising the electron density on N, so its lone pair accepts H+ more readily.
steps: The alkyl chain of butylamine pushes electron density towards the N atom (positive inductive effect).
This makes the N lone pair more available to accept a proton.
The butylammonium ion is a weaker acid than NH4+, since the alkyl group stabilises the positive charge less favourably for losing H+.
So the equilibrium C4H9NH2 + H2O to C4H9NH3+ + OH- lies further to the right than for NH3: butylamine is the stronger base.

questions.question: A dipeptide has molecular formula C7H12N2O3 and forms two amino acids on hydrolysis, one without a chiral centre. What is the structure of the other amino acid, which has a chiral centre? Options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: C: proline.
steps: Dipeptide C7H12N2O3 + H2O = C7H14N2O4 for the two amino acids together.
The amino acid without a chiral centre is glycine, C2H5NO2.
The other amino acid is C7H14N2O4 - C2H5NO2 = C5H9NO2.
Proline (C) is C5H9NO2 and has a chiral alpha carbon. A is C5H11NO2S, B is C5H11NO2 and D is C6H13NO2.

questions.question: Which of the synthetic polymers X, Y and Z are made by addition polymerisation? Formulae of X, Y and Z are shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: X and Y.
steps: X (-CH2-CHCl-) and Y (-CH2-CH(CONH2)-) have backbones of carbon atoms only, made from the alkenes CH2=CHCl and CH2=CHCONH2: addition polymers.
Z has amide links in the chain (-NH-CH2CH2-CO-), made by condensation of 3-aminopropanoic acid, so it is a condensation polymer.
So only X and Y are addition polymers: B.

questions.question: How many different types of amino acid have joined to form the octapeptide? Options: 4, 5, 6, 8.
questions.answer: B: 5 different amino acids.
steps: Split the chain at each peptide link and read the side chains from the N-terminus.
The sequence is glycine, glutamic acid, aspartic acid, aspartic acid, aspartic acid, tryptophan, aspartic acid, phenylalanine.
The different amino acids are glycine, glutamic acid, aspartic acid, tryptophan and phenylalanine, which is 5 types.

questions.question: Which functional group listed is not present in theobromine? A alkyl, B amide, C amine, D ketone. The skeletal structure is in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: ketone.
steps: The CH3 groups on the N atoms are alkyl groups, so A is present.
Both C=O groups are bonded directly to N (N-C=O), so they are amide groups, so B is present.
The ring nitrogens are amine-type nitrogens, so C is present.
A ketone needs a C=O between two carbon atoms, which does not occur here, so D is not present.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of serine? A 2-amino-2-carboxyethanol, B 2-amino-1-hydroxyethanoic acid, C 2-amino-1-hydroxypropanoic acid, D 2-amino-3-hydroxypropanoic acid.
questions.answer: D: 2-amino-3-hydroxypropanoic acid.
steps: Serine has a COOH group, so the parent is propanoic acid (3 carbons).
The NH2 group is on C2, next to the COOH.
The OH group is on C3, the CH2OH carbon.
Answer D.

questions.question: Which is the organic product of the reaction between serine and sodium hydroxide solution? The options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: H2N-CH(CH2OH)-COO^- Na+
steps: NaOH is a base and neutralises the acidic COOH group, giving the sodium carboxylate COO- Na+ and water.
The NH2 group is not protonated in alkaline solution, so it stays as NH2 (C and D with NH3+ are wrong).
The alcohol OH is much less acidic than COOH and is not deprotonated, so B and D are wrong.
The product is option A.

questions.question: Nylon 6-10 is made from a six-carbon diamine and a ten-carbon dicarboxylic acid. Which is its repeat unit? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: -NH-(CH2)6-NH-CO-(CH2)8-CO-
steps: Nylon 6,10 is made from a diamine with 6 carbons, H2N(CH2)6NH2, and a diacid with 10 carbons, HOOC(CH2)8COOH.
The diacid has 8 CH2 groups plus 2 carbonyl carbons, giving 10 carbons.
The repeat unit is -NH-(CH2)6-NH-CO-(CH2)8-CO-, option D.

questions.question: Which equation shows the formation of nitrous acid from sodium nitrite? A NaNO2 + HCl to HNO2 + NaCl, B NaNO3 + HCl to HNO3 + NaCl, C NaNO3 + HCl to HNO2 + NaClO, D NaNO2 + HCl to HNO2 + Na + Cl2.
questions.answer: A: NaNO2 + HCl to HNO2 + NaCl.
steps: Nitrous acid comes from nitrite ions (NO2-) and a strong acid.
NaNO2 + HCl to HNO2 + NaCl is balanced: Na, N, O, H and Cl on both sides.
Options B and C use nitrate, which gives HNO3 or the wrong product.
Option D is not balanced and gives chlorine, which is incorrect. Answer A.

questions.question: Which is the structure of the benzenediazonium ion formed from phenylamine and nitrous acid? Options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: C6H5-N+ with a triple bond to :N (lone pair on the terminal N).
steps: The benzenediazonium ion is C6H5-N2+, with the ring joined to the first N and a triple bond between the two N atoms.
The ring-bonded N has four bonds (one single, three in the triple bond), so it carries the + charge.
The terminal N has a triple bond and one lone pair, shown as N:, so D is correct.
A and C show a lone pair on the ring-bonded N, and B puts the + on the terminal N.

questions.question: Which reactant is required for the coupling reaction with the benzenediazonium ion to form chrysoidine?
questions.answer: A: benzene-1,3-diamine (1,3-diaminobenzene).
steps: Chrysoidine is 4-(phenylazo)benzene-1,3-diamine, with the azo group on a ring that carries two NH2 groups in a 1,3 relationship.
The benzenediazonium ion couples with the activated ring of benzene-1,3-diamine at the position para to one NH2 and ortho to the other.
So the coupling partner is benzene-1,3-diamine (A). B has an OH, C is a 1,2,4-triaminobenzene and D is already a diazonium salt.

questions.question: Which shows the structure of lysine as a solid, and in solution at high pH? Options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: the solid is the zwitterion (H3N+ and COO- on the alpha carbon, side-chain NH2); at high pH it is H2N and COO- with side-chain NH2.
steps: In the solid state an amino acid exists as a zwitterion: H3N+ and COO- on the alpha carbon, with the side-chain NH2 unchanged.
At high pH, the NH3+ loses H+ to become NH2, and the COO- and side-chain NH2 stay unchanged.
Only B shows both forms correctly.

questions.question: A repeat unit for a polyamide is shown. Which pair of monomers makes this polymer? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: H2N(CH2)6NH2 and HOOC(CH2)4COOH
steps: The repeat unit is -NH-(CH2)6-NH-CO-(CH2)4-CO-, so the N side comes from a diamine with 6 carbons.
The C=O side has (CH2)4 between two C=O, so the diacid is HOOC(CH2)4COOH (hexanedioic acid).
The monomers are H2N(CH2)6NH2 and HOOC(CH2)4COOH, option A (nylon 6,6).

questions.question: Four compounds W, X, Y and Z are shown. Which is an optically active amino acid?
questions.answer: C: compound Y (alanine).
steps: An optically active amino acid needs an NH2 and a COOH, and a chiral carbon with four different groups.
W has no NH2, X has two CH3 groups on the central carbon, and Z has two COOH groups, so none of them is chiral.
Y has COOH, NH2, CH3 and H on the central carbon: it is alanine and is chiral, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Which compound does not have the same number of peaks in the low-resolution proton NMR and the 13C NMR spectrum? Options: W, X, Y, Z.
questions.answer: C: compound Y.
steps: W (CH3)2CHCOOH: 3 environments in both spectra (CH3 x2 equivalent, CH, COOH).
X (CH3)2C(NH2)COOH: 3 in 1H NMR (CH3, NH2, COOH) and 3 in 13C (CH3, C, COOH).
Y CH3CH(NH2)COOH: 4 in 1H NMR (CH3, CH, NH2, COOH) but only 3 in 13C NMR (CH3, CH, COOH), so the numbers differ.
Z CH3C(NH2)(COOH)2: 3 in 1H NMR (CH3, NH2, two equivalent COOH) and 3 in 13C NMR (CH3, C, COOH).
The answer is Y: C.

questions.question: Deduce the molecular formula of procaine.
questions.answer: C13H20N2O2
steps: Carbon: 6 in the ring, 1 in C=O, 2 in OCH2CH2, 4 in the two ethyl groups, which makes 13.
Hydrogen: 4 on the ring, 2 in NH2, 4 in OCH2CH2 and 10 in the two ethyl groups, which makes 20.
Nitrogen 2 and oxygen 2, so the formula is C13H20N2O2.

questions.question: Identify, by name or formula, the two reagents needed for Step 1 of the procaine synthesis.
questions.answer: Chloromethane (CH3Cl) and aluminium chloride (AlCl3, anhydrous, as catalyst).
steps: Step 1 puts a methyl group on benzene: a Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
Reagents are CH3Cl (chloromethane) and anhydrous AlCl3 (halogen carrier catalyst), which makes the CH3+ electrophile.
Benzene + CH3Cl -> methylbenzene + HCl.

questions.question: For Step 2 of the procaine synthesis, draw the mechanism, including formation of a suitable electrophile and regeneration of the catalyst, with curly arrows.
questions.answer: Electrophilic substitution: NO2+ attacks methylbenzene para to the CH3 to form an arenium ion, which loses H+ to give 4-nitromethylbenzene, and the H2SO4 catalyst is regenerated.
steps: Electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4- (H2SO4 protonates the OH of HNO3, then water is lost, leaving NO2+). Show curly arrows for these steps.
Curly arrow from the delocalised ring (a C=C) to the N atom of NO2+, at the carbon para to the CH3.
The intermediate is a horseshoe (partial ring) with a + charge, and the carbon bearing NO2 also has an H.
Curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring, so H+ leaves and aromaticity is restored, giving 4-nitromethylbenzene.
Catalyst regenerated: H+ + HSO4- -> H2SO4.

questions.question: For Step 5 of the procaine synthesis, name the type of reaction and draw the skeletal formula of the reagent.
questions.answer: Nucleophilic addition-elimination (esterification); reagent 2-(diethylamino)ethanol, HOCH2CH2N(CH2CH3)2.
steps: Step 5 converts an acyl chloride into an ester, so the reagent is an alcohol containing the diethylamino group.
The reagent is HO-CH2-CH2-N(CH2CH3)2, 2-(diethylamino)ethanol.
Skeletal formula: HO attached to a two-carbon zig-zag chain ending in N, with two ethyl groups on N.
The O lone pair of the alcohol attacks the C=O carbon and Cl- is lost (nucleophilic addition-elimination).

questions.question: Identify, by name or formula, the reagents required for Step 6 of the procaine synthesis.
questions.answer: Tin and concentrated HCl (heat under reflux), then NaOH(aq).
steps: Step 6 reduces the nitro group NO2 to an amine NH2.
Reagents: Sn with concentrated HCl, heated under reflux, then NaOH(aq) to release the free amine.
Hydrogen with a nickel or platinum catalyst is an alternative.

questions.question: Explain why the two nitrogen atoms in procaine have different basicity.
questions.answer: The tertiary alkyl amine N is more basic because its lone pair is available, whereas the aromatic NH2 lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.
steps: The nitrogen in the diethylamino group is bonded to alkyl groups, which push electron density towards N (positive inductive effect).
This makes its lone pair more available to accept H+, so it is the stronger base.
The nitrogen of the aromatic NH2 has its lone pair delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept H+.
So the two nitrogen atoms differ in basicity: the diethylamino N is the stronger base.

questions.question: Draw the structure of procaine hydrochloride, showing how the hydrogen ion attaches to the molecule.
questions.answer: Procaine with the diethylamino N protonated: [H2N-C6H4-COO-CH2CH2-NH+(CH2CH3)2] Cl-.
steps: The more basic nitrogen is the tertiary N of the diethylamino group, so H+ attaches there.
The N lone pair forms a dative covalent bond to H+, giving N+ with four bonds (H, two ethyl groups, CH2CH2O...).
The aromatic NH2 stays unchanged, and Cl- is the counter-ion.

questions.question: Explain why procaine hydrochloride is more soluble in aqueous solutions such as blood plasma than procaine.
questions.answer: Procaine hydrochloride is an ionic salt, so its ions form strong ion-dipole attractions with polar water molecules and dissolve more readily than neutral procaine.
steps: Protonating the amine gives an ionic salt, containing a positively charged ammonium group and a Cl- ion.
Ions are attracted to the partial charges of water molecules (ion-dipole attraction) and are hydrated.
Neutral procaine interacts with water only through weaker dipole and hydrogen-bond interactions.
So the hydrochloride dissolves more readily in aqueous blood plasma.

questions.topic: Number of Molecules in a Dose
questions.question: Lidocaine cartridges are 2.2 cm3 and contain 44 mg. Calculate the number of lidocaine molecules in a 1.5 cm3 dose (molar mass 234 g mol-1).
questions.answer: 7.7 x 10^19 molecules
steps: Answer to 2 significant figures: 7.7 x 10^19 molecules.

questions.question: Which reagents are mixed with hydrochloric acid to produce the benzenediazonium ion? A C6H5NH2 and NaNO2, B C6H5NO2 and NaNO2, C C6H5NO2 and NaNO3, D C6H5NH2 and NaNO3.
questions.answer: A: C6H5NH2 (phenylamine) and NaNO2.
steps: The diazonium ion is made from a primary aromatic amine, phenylamine C6H5NH2.
Sodium nitrite with HCl forms nitrous acid in situ, which diazotises the amine.
Nitrobenzene (C6H5NO2) is not an amine, and nitrate (NaNO3) cannot form nitrous acid.
Answer A.

questions.question: Which reagents and conditions prepare the yellow dye 4-phenyldiazenylphenol from benzenediazonium ion? A phenol in acid at 25 C, B phenol in alkaline at 25 C, C phenol in acid at 5 C, D phenol in alkaline at 5 C.
questions.answer: D: phenol dissolved in alkaline solution at 5 C.
steps: Coupling needs the highly activated phenoxide ion, formed in alkaline solution.
Acidic conditions leave phenol unionised, so coupling is slow.
The diazonium ion is kept cold (about 5 C) to avoid decomposition.
Answer D.

questions.question: What is the repeat unit of the water-soluble polymer poly(ethenol)? Options are structures in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: -CH2-CH(OH)-
steps: Poly(ethenol) is an addition polymer from ethenol, CH2=CH-OH, so the repeat unit has a two-carbon backbone.
One carbon is CH2 and the other carries H and OH: -CH2-CH(OH)-.
This is option B (top row H, H and bottom row H, OH).

questions.question: Draw the skeletal structure of trimethylamine, C3H9N.
questions.answer: (CH3)3N: a central N atom bonded to three CH3 groups, with one lone pair on N.
steps: C3H9N has three carbons and nine hydrogens, so it has three CH3 groups.
All three CH3 groups are bonded to a single N atom.
N has a lone pair, so it has three bonds plus one lone pair (trigonal pyramidal).
Draw the N with three lines to C atoms and the lone pair shown.

questions.question: Identify the class of amine to which trimethylamine belongs.
questions.answer: Tertiary amine: the N is bonded to three alkyl groups.
steps: Primary amines have one alkyl group on N, secondary have two, tertiary have three.
Trimethylamine has three CH3 groups bonded to N.
So it is a tertiary amine.

questions.question: Trimethylamine is a gas at room temperature but readily dissolves in water. Draw a diagram of the intermolecular force that leads to its solubility, including dipoles and lone pairs.
questions.answer: Hydrogen bonding between the lone pair on N of trimethylamine (delta-) and an O-H hydrogen of water (delta+), shown as a dotted line.
steps: The N atom has a lone pair and is partially negative (delta-).
The H atoms of water are partially positive (delta+) because O-H bonds are polar.
Draw the N lone pair pointing to the H of an O-H group of water with a dotted hydrogen bond line.
Show dipoles on N-H, O-H and the lone pairs, labelled delta- and delta+.

questions.question: Write an ionic equation to show how trimethylamine acts as a base in aqueous solution (state symbols not required).
questions.answer: (CH3)3N + H2O to (CH3)3NH+ + OH-
steps: Trimethylamine accepts a proton from water using its N lone pair.
Water loses H+ and forms OH- ions.
This produces the alkaline solution: (CH3)3N + H2O to (CH3)3NH+ + OH-.

questions.question: Trimethylamine N-oxide (C3H9NO) has a concentration of 3.90 x 10^-6 mol dm-3 in blood. An adult has 5.00 dm3 of blood. Calculate the mass in grams of trimethylamine N-oxide in the blood.
steps: Three significant figures, as in the data.

questions.question: Briefly describe how trimethylamine is separated from other chemicals in an air sample by gas chromatography.
questions.answer: The sample is vaporised and carried by an inert gas through a column with a stationary liquid phase; components partition between the two phases and separate by their different affinities and volatilities.
steps: The sample is injected and vaporised, then carried through the column by an inert carrier gas (the mobile phase).
Components distribute between the gas phase and the stationary liquid phase coating the column.
Compounds with weaker interaction with the stationary phase, or higher volatility, move faster.
Each component elutes at a characteristic retention time, so trimethylamine is separated from the others.

questions.question: Label the x-axis on the HPLC chromatogram used to measure trimethylamine and trimethylamine N-oxide.
questions.answer: Retention time (min).
steps: In a chromatogram the x-axis shows the time each compound takes to elute (retention time).
The unit is minutes.
The y-axis shows the detector response (peak height).

questions.question: Name the analytical technique that can be used with either GC or HPLC to identify the compound responsible for each peak.
questions.answer: Mass spectrometry (GC-MS or LC-MS).
steps: Mass spectrometry measures the mass-to-charge ratio of ions from each separated compound.
Coupling it to GC or HPLC (GC-MS or LC-MS) identifies the compound eluting at each retention time.

questions.question: Which is the repeat unit of the polymer formed from the monomers shown? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: C: -CO-C6H4-CO-NH-(CH2)3-NH- as the repeat unit.
steps: Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and propane-1,3-diamine form a polyamide by condensation, losing water.
The repeat unit starts with a C=O (from the acid) and ends with an N-H (from the amine): -CO-C6H4-CO-NH-CH2CH2CH2-NH-.
B ends with an extra C=O, D starts with an extra NH, and A joins the chain through a ketone C=O instead of an amide link, so only C is correct.

questions.question: Which are the reagents and conditions for the reaction shown? A K2Cr2O7 with H+ and reflux, B LiAlH4 in dry ether, C H2 gas at high temperature, D Sn, concentrated HCl and reflux.
questions.answer: D: Sn and concentrated HCl, heated under reflux (then NaOH).
steps: The reaction reduces the nitro group NO2 on the ring to NH2.
Tin with concentrated hydrochloric acid under reflux is the standard reagent for reducing nitroarenes to arylamines, with NaOH added afterwards to release the amine.
K2Cr2O7/H+ is an oxidising agent. LiAlH4 does not give the amine cleanly from a nitroarene. H2 gas needs a catalyst, not just high temperature.

questions.topic: Product of Amine with Acyl Chloride
questions.question: Which product forms when butylamine reacts with ethanoyl chloride? A ethanamide, B butanamide, C N-butylethanamide, D N-ethylbutanamide.
questions.answer: C: N-butylethanamide.
steps: Butylamine's N attacks the C of ethanoyl chloride's C=O.
Cl- is eliminated and the N-H proton is lost (addition-elimination).
The butyl group stays on N and the ethanoyl group forms the C=O: CH3CONHC4H9.
This is N-butylethanamide, option C.

questions.question: At what pH would phenylalanine have the structure shown? Options: pH 2, pH 6, pH 10, pH 14. The structure is shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: pH 6
steps: The structure has NH3+ and COO-, so it is the zwitterion.
The zwitterion dominates near the isoelectric point, around pH 6.
At pH 2 the COO- would be protonated (COOH), and at pH 10 and 14 the NH3+ would lose H+ to give NH2.
